title: Head in the Cloud? What's on the Horizon for Offline Intelligence
blurb: Subscription fatigue? There should be an app for that. Explores the consequences of cloud-based assistive technology delivery — the subscription trap, recurring cost burden, and what offline and on-device AI alternatives exist today and on the horizon.

featured_slides.note: Designed for the professional sector, LiveScribe Smartpens have long been a staple for student disability offices because they combine paper-based notetaking with on-device audio recording and intuitive tap-to-play recall. This original configuration has been superseded by newer models with smartphone app integrations which illustrates the tension between the stable feature set desirable in the context of Assistive Technology and accommodations versus the dynamics of continuous feature updates and enhancement.

The Kurzweil Reading Machine is emblematic of early Assistive Technology - purpose-built and expensive, with custom interfaces requiring intensive user and operator training. The question then is whether the benefits of technology evolution away from this model toward more affordable, device-independent, intuitive access is necessarily tied to the cloud and subscription-based delivery model.

The trend across every modality — language, vision, audio — is that the smallest model capable of a given task keeps shrinking in size and associated resource demand. That compression suggests offline assistive technology uses will continue to emerge and promote new forms of access outside of established patterns of the past and present.
